analysis.one_liner: Expands public reporting of toxic chemical use and releases and requires polluting facilities to write pollution prevention plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote in the Senate and died when the 102nd Congress ended, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have greatly expanded the Toxics Release Inventory, the public database where companies report the toxic chemicals they use and release. It would have added 250 chemicals to the reporting list, extended reporting to facilities outside manufacturing — mines, utilities, pipelines, railroads, truckers, airlines, hospitals, colleges, and federal facilities — and required companies to file pollution prevention plans with public summaries. It would also have given EPA and state inspectors stronger access to facilities and created grants for local emergency planning.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near facilities that handle toxic chemicals, who would get far more complete information about what is being used and released in their communities. Workers and consumers would also benefit from required toxic-use-reduction planning, and local emergency planners would receive federal grants.

how_it_helps.text: Adds 250 toxic chemicals to the reporting list, including Clean Air Act ozone-depleting substances, known and probable human carcinogens, restricted pesticides, and drinking-water contaminants, with an automatic list that takes effect if EPA fails to act [S2] [S3].

Extends reporting beyond manufacturing to facilities in mining, oil and gas extraction, utilities, pipelines, rail, motor freight, air and water transport, hospitals, colleges, testing labs, and federal facilities, and directs EPA to add more industries that pose comparable threats [S2] [S3].

Requires reporting of source reduction practices, recycling and treatment amounts, materials accounting data, and three-year pollution prevention goals, so the public can see whether facilities are actually reducing toxics rather than just releasing them [S2] [S3].
Requires each covered facility to prepare a pollution prevention plan every three years, with summaries and annual progress reports made available to the public [S2] [S3].

Gives EPA and state officials authority to enter facilities, inspect records, and take samples, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for refusing access, and adds criminal penalties for knowingly violating the pollution prevention planning requirements [S3].

Creates a grant program, authorized at $12 million per year through fiscal 1996, for states, local governments, and local emergency planning committees, with 75 percent of each state grant passed through to localities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that handle toxic chemicals — chemical makers, energy and mining companies, transportation and utility operators, hospitals, colleges, and federal agencies — would bear the cost of expanded reporting, materials accounting, and periodic pollution prevention planning.

drawbacks.text: Thousands of newly covered facilities, including hospitals, colleges, and small service businesses like auto body shops and exterminators, would face new reporting and paperwork costs [S3].

The bill does not mandate actual emission cuts: pollution prevention plans contain voluntary pledges, and EPA is expressly barred from requiring that any particular pollution prevention measure be implemented or any performance standard be achieved [S3].

The President could exempt any executive branch facility from reporting for one year at a time, renewable indefinitely, which would allow federal facilities to avoid the same disclosure required of private ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is broad community information about toxic chemical use and releases, plus pressure toward prevention; the costs are compliance paperwork spread across many industries, and the strongest honest criticism is that the centerpiece plans are voluntary pledges rather than enforceable reductions, with a presidential exemption carved out for federal facilities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in March 1992, never received any hearing, markup, or floor action, and expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Dave Durenberger, a Minnesota Republican, introduced the bill on March 17, 1992, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1] [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and there were no floor votes before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that would have faced expanded disclosure and planning requirements kept the status quo, and the public did not get the broader chemical reporting the bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Dave Durenberger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting the bill expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican senator sponsored the bill with no cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and industrial chemical users
industries.note: The bill would have added 250 chemicals to public release reporting and required materials accounting and pollution prevention plans, exposing the full scope of their toxic chemical use. Its findings note the existing inventory had already revealed far larger releases than expected and pushed companies to cut them.

industries.industry: Energy, utilities, mining, and oil and gas extraction
industries.note: These sectors would have been newly subject to toxic release reporting for the first time. Their emissions and chemical handling would become publicly searchable.

industries.industry: Transportation and warehousing (rail, trucking, air, water, pipelines)
industries.note: Newly covered by reporting requirements, including removal of the exemption for transporting covered toxic chemicals. Compliance would mean disclosing chemical shipments and handling across the supply chain.

Institutions would face new reporting duties but are also sources of toxic chemical releases that the public currently cannot see. Some could qualify for limited applicability of the detailed reporting provisions.

Mandatory pollution prevention plans, feasibility studies, and required training and seminars would have created steady demand for plan preparation and training providers. The services exist to help facilities comply and reduce toxics.
